items.descriptionOriginal: P atty Spillman and her husband farm over 400 acres of corn, soybeans and wheat in central Ohio. Both have lived in the area all their lives; his family has been on the land since 1861. In 2023, a developer proposed a data center on a nearby farm. “[The community] fought them off,” she says. “But I always kind of knew that just because the one data center had left, that didn’t mean it was going to be gone forever. Someone else was going to be right on their heels.” She was right. Less than two years later, another developer started moving forward with plans for a much larger data center, located across the street from her farm. Headwaters, a Texas-based company, wanted to annex land in Pleasant Township (where Spillman lives) and nearby Jackson Township for a 300-plus acre facility in Grove City. This is a story playing out in communities across the U.S., where A.I. demands have rapidly accelerated the need for data centers, along with the extraordinary amounts of water and energy that they consume. But residents are pushing back, advocating for more community input, insisting that the data facilities cover the full cost of locating there (such as local grid infrastructure upgrades), and even calling for outright moratoriums. Patty Spillman and her husband on their land. Courtesy of Protect Grove City Crucially, these movements don’t break along party lines: Republicans, Democrats and Independents across the country are mad — and they’re working together to block development. This bipartisan push is particularly notable at a time of intense polarization. There’s not much that people from different political parties can agree on, but according to a recent poll from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, very few people want an A.I. data center in their community. That’s certainly true in Grove City, a Republican-leaning suburb of Columbus, where people of all parties opposed the Headwaters development. The nature of this coalition isn’t totally unprecedented, says Megan Mullin, a professor of public policy at the University of California, Los Angeles. “In so many ways, data center battles look like land use battles that have come before,” she says. “Battles over housing developments, wind farms or gas pipelines — we consistently see people come together across party lines to try to keep their community looking the way it’s always looked, and to fight back against what they perceive as harmful draws on community resources.” Mullin says a big difference now is that all of these hyper-local fights are happening at once. While one or two bipartisan coalitions on a land use debate wouldn’t rise to the level of national news, hundreds of them happening simultaneously around the country does. “That allows these local disputes to be connected to something national, and it also allows concrete movement building.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] In Ohio, residents of Grove City and the surrounding townships quickly mobilized once they realized that Headwaters wanted to site a data center in their community. “We got organized,” says Jen Belt, one of the four people behind Protect Grove City , which actively opposed the development. “Most people weren’t even aware that this was a thing. We taped flyers to every home within a three-mile radius of the developer’s site. We encouraged people to come to all of the council meetings.” They also worked on gathering signatures to encourage the Grove City city council to pass a moratorium. (Pleasant Township and Jackson Township had already passed moratoriums in the first half of 2026.) Ultimately, Belt says, they gathered more than 4,000 signatures for the online petition. Their efforts worked. In June, the city council passed a one-year moratorium on data center development. But Belt and her neighbors know it is temporary, and developers will come back once the year is up. So they have put a Community Consent Amendment (CCA) on the upcoming November ballot. If passed, it will require residents’ approval before any large-scale development can break ground. (While it’s geared toward data centers, it’s written to apply to all heavy industry.) Belt, like Spillman, lives in Pleasant Township, which she calls “suburban rural.” But she scoffs at the idea that the issue doesn’t impact her just because she’s not within city limits. “This is property that will be annexed from my town into Grove City,” says Belt, a registered Democrat. “It’s literally in my backyard. So it does affect us.” Spillman, a lifelong Republican, agrees: “This is our community. This is our neighborhood, and none of us can vote on any of this, because we don’t live in Grove City proper, but we still consider Grove City our home.” Data centers have been going up in earnest for the last decade, built to support the rapid growth of the cloud. Opposition has existed nearly as long . But as A.I. usage has exploded in the last several years, the demand for data centers has rapidly accelerated as well. The post Finally, Something Americans Agree On! appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

Ο αέρας του Δελχί δείχνει πόσο γρήγορα μπορούν να αλλάξουν τα πράγματα. Στις 4 μ.μ. της Τρίτης 20 Οκτωβρίου, το Κεντρικό Συμβούλιο Ελέγχου Ρύπανσης έθεσε τον Δείκτη Ποιότητας Αέρα (AQI) στο 179, ο οποίος θεωρείται μέτριος…
items.descriptionOriginal: The cool, quiet hour after dawn feels like the best time to step outside in October, yet AIIMS says pollution stays highest in the early morning until about 8:30 or 9 am. Delhi's air shows how quickly things can turn. At 4 pm on Tuesday, 20 October, the Central Pollution Control Board put the Air Quality Index (AQI) at 179, which counts as moderate. By 7 am the next day, the Air Quality Early Warning System showed 219, which counts as poor, and it forecast 342 for 22 October. The invisible lid above the city The explanation lies in physics. Normally, temperature falls with height, so air near the ground mixes and carries pollutants upwards. University of Reading researchers Ankit Bhandekar and Laura Wilcox explain that a temperature inversion reverses this, placing warmer air above colder air like a lid on a pot. Pollutants stay near the ground, and the mixing height, the level up to which they can disperse, shrinks from about one kilometre in summer to a few hundred metres in winter. The lid sits lowest after dark. Sarath Guttikunda, founder of UrbanEmissions.Info, told Frontline that in November and December the inversion height can fall below 50 metres at night and hover around 200 to 500 metres by day. As the sun climbs, the layer lifts and the smog thins, which is why the early hours feel the worst. A bowl that holds on to smoke Delhi's geography makes this even worse. The city sits in the Indo-Gangetic plains, with the Himalayas to the north and the smaller Aravalli range to the south, which help create a natural bowl. Delhi's location between the Himalayas and the Aravallis, coupled with slow winds and little rain, allows pollution to linger. Photograph: (AI-Generated collage) The Himalayas block air from flowing northward, so pollution must travel across northern India before it finds an exit over the Bay of Bengal. The monsoon rains that cleanse the air from July to September have gone by October, and winds slow down. Small shifts in weather can therefore tip the balance fast. Bhandekar and Wilcox note that on 5 January, 2025, favourable winds allowed authorities to lift some restrictions, yet by 15 January calmer winds and falling temperatures forced the city's strictest curbs. Delhi had not gained more cars, factories or construction sites from one week to the next. The Centre for Science and Environment also found something similar in winter 2023, when slow winds appeared to drive the most smog episodes in six years even though stubble fires in Punjab and Haryana nearly matched 2022. Solutions that follow the weather If weather decides when pollution turns, the Reading researchers argue, policy should follow the forecast rather than chase the smog. They suggest tightening construction restrictions when inversions are predicted, even on seemingly clear days, and designing measures for the whole Indo-Gangetic plains, since many of India's most polluted cities share the same conditions. Calm winds and falling temperatures can intensify smog even without an increase in vehicles, factories or construction. Photograph: ( The Print ) Delhi's Graded Response Action Plan already lets authorities act in advance on forecasts, with curbs ranging from dust control to limits on construction and vehicle movement. The other lever sits upwind, because smoke from stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana , where farmers clear fields quickly for wheat sowing, adds to the load each October and November. Some farmers avoid it by sowing wheat directly with a Happy Seeder , spraying a waste decomposer solution on straw , or selling paddy straw for conversion into fuel pellets . What you can do this season First, treat the cool early hours as the risky ones, since AIIMS advises staying indoors at peak hours and choosing indoor exercise over outdoor runs or cycling. Second, check the AQI daily on the SAMEER app, which AIIMS recommends, and wear an N95 mask if you step out. Third, take extra care of children, older people and anyone with heart or lung conditions, whom the AIIMS advisory flags as most at risk. Fourth, skip driving once a week to trim local emissions, as AIIMS suggests. The advice does not reach everyone equally. Business Standard reports that an air purifier costing ₹12,000 to ₹15,000 is out of reach for many informal workers, and that indoor air can still hold up to 70% of outdoor PM2.5 without sealed windows and purifiers. That is why forecast-led curbs and cleaner fields matter as much as personal habits. Delhi cannot change the bowl it sits in or the chill that settles each night, but it can change what it puts into the air beneath the lid. With poor air forecast for 21 to 23 October, the next crisp, quiet dawn is better read as a warning than a relief. Sources: 1. ' Delhi's air quality slips to poor category, forecast to worsen further ': by Akshita Singh for Business Standard, Published on 21 October, 2026 2. ' How weather patterns and faraway mountains make Delhi the world's most polluted megacity ': by Ankit Bhandekar and Laura Wilcox for The Conversation (republished by Newslaundry), Published on 3 March, 2025 3. ' Delhi's Air Pollution Explained! ': by R. Ramachandran for Frontline, Published on 9 December, 2016 4. ' Delhi's annual battle with air pollution: Aiims issues health advisory ': by Barkha Mathur for Business Standard, Published on 6 November, 2025 5. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Urban Woodlands and Mental Health are Connected, According to a Major Scottish Study Reading Time: 3 minutes A major five-year study finds that urban woodlands and mental health are closely connected, with well-kept city woods linked to fewer antidepressant prescriptions in Scotland’s poorest neighborhoods. Urban woodlands and mental health appear to move together, according to new research from the Universities of Edinburgh and Glasgow. Scientists tracked more than 129,000 people across Scotland over five years. They found that people living close to improved woodlands used less medication for depression and anxiety. The study , published in The Lancet Planetary Health, used National Health Service prescription records alongside census data. Researchers compared people living within a 10-minute walk of an upgraded woodland to those living farther away. The gap in medication use was substantial. People near a well-maintained, welcoming woodland were 10% less likely to be prescribed antidepressants. They were also 6% less likely to need anti-anxiety medication. That pattern held even after researchers accounted for income, demographics, and other factors known to affect mental health. This is one of the largest studies of its kind linking urban woodlands and mental health outcomes. The woodland upgrades came through Scottish Forestry’s Woods In and Around Towns program (WIAT). Funding paid for new footpaths, better signage, and community events in areas that needed it most. The program specifically targeted socially and financially disadvantaged communities. These are often the places with the least access to quality parks and green space to begin with. By focusing improvements there, researchers could measure whether fixing a woodland actually changed people’s health, not just their surroundings. What makes this research especially convincing is how it tracked people over time. When someone moved closer to an improved woodland, their need for medication tended to drop. When they moved farther away, that protective effect faded. The connection between urban woodlands and mental health was strengthened with a telling finding: when people moved closer to improved woodlands, their need for antidepressants fell, and when they moved away, the protective effect faded with them. Photo by Vitaly Gariev on Pexels. That detail matters. Earlier studies often compared different people living in different neighborhoods at a single moment. This approach made it hard to know whether nature improved mental health, or whether healthier people simply chose to live near woodlands already. By following the same individuals as their circumstances changed, researchers could rule out that explanation. Professor Catharine Ward Thompson, who led the study at the University of Edinburgh’s OPENspace Research Centre, said the findings offer stronger evidence on the link between urban woodlands and mental health than earlier research managed to provide. She added that the benefits may help reduce mental health inequalities across the population. Dr. Scott Ogletree, who carried out the analysis, said the project marks the first time mental health service data has been linked to a long-term national urban forestry program. He noted that relatively modest investments in local green space can meaningfully improve people’s wellbeing. Nature-based programs like WIAT, he said, can support broader efforts to improve mental health. The scale of the problem makes this evidence timely. Around one in eight people worldwide live with a mental health condition, and people in poorer communities are often hit hardest. These same communities often have the least access to high-quality woodlands and parks. Scotland’s government has pointed to this research as support for its wider environmental goals. Officials cited a target of creating 18,000 hectares of new woodland every year by 2029 to 2030. That commitment extends to urban tree planting aimed at improving air quality and quality of life. The connection between urban woodlands and mental health also fits into a broader pattern seen elsewhere, where community-driven tree planting has helped cool neighborhoods and improve public health by giving residents a direct role in restoring local green space. Programs like these suggest the benefits of investing in trees extend well beyond any single country. The research team behind the Scottish study has spent more than 20 years gathering evidence on the social value of local woodlands, working alongside Scottish Forestry and Forest Research. Their latest findings add a rigorous, long-term dataset to a growing conversation about nature-based public health policy. Funding came from the Economic and Social Research Council and the GroundsWell Consortium, a UK research partnership focused on how green and blue spaces reduce health inequalities. None of this suggests woodlands replace clinical care for depression or anxiety. What it does suggest is that a safe, welcoming patch of trees within walking distance can meaningfully shift the odds. As more cities weigh where to spend limited public money, the growing evidence on urban woodlands and mental health makes a strong case for choosing the trail over the parking lot. The post How Urban Woodlands and Mental Health are Connected, According to a Major Scottish Study appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: What happens when two generations open their doors to one another? In West Philadelphia, a small but growing program called Second Story Collective is bringing college students and older residents together through shared housing, creating unexpected friendships along the way. For Ms. Julia, a retired nursing assistant who has lived in her neighborhood for more than 50 years, welcoming 22-year-old Drexel University student Jackson Tignor into her home has brought new companionship and laughter. In return, Jackson has found more than an affordable place to live -- he's discovered a sense of belonging and a deeper connection to the community around him. Through everyday moments of shared meals, conversations, and helping hands, the program is quietly challenging loneliness, housing insecurity, and the divisions that too often separate generations. Sometimes, building a stronger community begins with something as simple as opening a door.

items.descriptionOriginal: Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease? Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells. Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively healthy.

items.descriptionOriginal: At a Ganpati gathering in Mumbai, lunch was over and everyone was waiting for dessert. The thalis had been cleared, conversations had moved on, and there was only one thing left to do: bring out the kheer. Except this time, there was something unusual in the cutlery. Niki Rai, who had organised the gathering, asked her guests to hold on to their spoons instead of throwing them away. A few eyebrows went up. She had already told everyone that these were edible, but people were still understandably unsure. Then came dessert. "Now this is your biscuit," Rai told the children, handing them their dessert with the spoon. The reaction was almost immediate. The children started biting into the spoons, treating them less like cutlery and more like a crunchy snack. The adults were more hesitant, watching first to see if it really worked. Soon, however, others wanted a taste too. "It was quite a spectacle, but it was worth it," Rai recalls. The spoons had been made by Mumbai-based startup Edybites, which is trying to tackle a very ordinary problem: what happens to a disposable spoon after the few minutes it spends helping us finish a meal? Its answer is simple enough to eat. Founded by Rupesh K Sanghvi in 2022, Edybites makes edible spoons using a millet and flour-based formulation. The idea is that the spoon can become part of the meal rather than another piece of waste to be thrown away. If it is not eaten, the product is designed to naturally decompose. After 88 failed attempts, Sanghvi refined the spoon's shape, texture and sturdiness to make it practical for everyday use. But turning that simple idea into a spoon that could hold its own through a meal was another story. It had to be sturdy enough to carry food, pleasant enough to eat and practical enough to make at a price people would accept. The idea began with a spoon and a piece of khakra For Sanghvi, the thought first came during the COVID-19 lockdown. With fewer services and errands available, everyday household work suddenly meant doing much more oneself. One day, after preparing a meal and looking at a sink full of utensils, he found himself eating with his fingers because there was no clean spoon left. That brought back a familiar Gujarati food memory: khakra. "If we can finish our last meal of dal khichdi with a combination of khakra," he thought, could something similar be made in the form of a spoon? The thought stayed with him. It also connected with something Sanghvi had observed during his more than 17 years in the aviation and travel industry. Having worked in sales and business development with airlines including Malaysia Airlines, Flydubai, Malindo Air and Kuwait Airways, he had seen how much disposable material moved through a flight. Once a flight landed, used food packaging and cutlery had to be discarded. Some meal components could not be reused because of safety and airline policies, even when they had not been consumed. The edible spoons are designed to hold food during a meal and can be eaten afterwards, reducing the need for disposable plastic cutlery. For Sanghvi, that raised a broader question : could at least one small part of the meal be made differently? He initially imagined the spoon being used with yoghurt, pastries, desserts or dishes such as dal khichdi and sambar rice on flights. Aviation remains one of the sectors he is interested in, alongside hospitals, institutional catering and events. The larger idea, however, is not simply to tell people to use less plastic. It is to make the alternative convenient enough that people actually use it. Making a spoon that does not fall apart That turned out to be the difficult part. Sanghvi says he failed 88 times while developing the spoon. Each version had to be tested for its shape, size, weight, and sturdiness. It needed to be strong enough to hold food, but not so hard that eating it became uncomfortable. The formulation uses a combination of sorghum, corn flour, and wheat flour, along with other ingredients. Sanghvi says the precise recipe is proprietary, but the millet and flour-based formulation is central to giving the spoon its structure. Too much flour, and the spoon could become soggy quickly. Too much firmness, and it could become difficult to bite. The team also experimented with flavours. Chocolate emerged as one of the main variants, particularly because it pairs naturally with vanilla ice cream. Edybites offers different flavours, including chocolate, which pairs well with desserts such as vanilla ice cream. That makes dessert one of the easiest places to introduce the concept. A person may be more willing to eat a spoon after finishing a bowl of ice cream than rethink every piece of cutlery used during an entire meal. There is also a practical reason Edybites has focused on spoons rather than trying to replace every disposable food item at once. Sanghvi says other edible products, such as cups, can face challenges when they are expected to hold liquids for longer periods. With tea or coffee, for instance, the material can soften or affect the eating experience. The spoon offers a smaller, more manageable starting point. The product has a shelf life of about three months without refrigeration, with the team working towards extending it further. It is made under a contractual manufacturing arrangement, with attention to hygiene and the heating process required to form the spoon. The finished spoons are individually covered and packed in boxes designed to minimise breakage during transportation. The product also requires the relevant food safety certification, including an FSSAI licence. When the spoon reached a real dining table For Niki Rai, the real test came not in a product demonstration but at a family gathering. Rai, a learning and development professional and executive coach, had first heard about the product through a friend. She was curious but wanted to try it herself before recommending it to others. When she eventually used Edybites spoons at a Ganpati gathering, she served them alongside a regular thali and asked guests to try them with the sabzi. Later, she brought them out again with kheer. The children needed little convincing. "For kids, it was like a biscuit," she says. For adults, the experience was more about getting used to the idea. Rai says the spoon felt similar to a regular spoon and was comfortable to use, although its smaller size meant it could not hold a large quantity of food. She found it particularly suited to desserts, while children could use it for foods such as porridge too. At a Ganpati gathering in Mumbai, Niki Rai introduced Edybites spoons to guests, with children happily biting into them like biscuits after dessert. What stood out most to her was not just that the spoon was edible, but that it did not feel like a compromise. For Rai, taste was important. She also liked that the ingredients included grains such as jowar and wheat, along with fenugreek, rather than making the spoon feel like an entirely separate object that happened to be sustainable. Once the children started eating theirs, curiosity took over. The parents who had initially been apprehensive began joining in. Soon, Rai says, people were asking for extra spoons. Since then, she has continued recommending the product at events and gatherings, including while travelling. Making the sustainable choice practical There is, however, a catch. An Edybites spoon currently costs around Rs 7-8, according to Sanghvi. That is considerably more than a conventional disposable spoon, making price one of the biggest hurdles to getting people to make the switch. After all, when a plastic spoon costs a fraction of that, convincing someone to pay more for something they will eat or discard after one meal is not easy. Sanghvi has seen this play out in the conversations around the product. "However rich you are, at one point you would think, just to have a spoon, why should I pay seven rupees?" he says. That is why Edybites has not tried to rush into the mass market. Since November last year, when the startup began seeing stronger market traction, it has sold or distributed more than 5,100 spoons. For now, Sanghvi is taking a gradual route, exploring events, institutional catering, hospitals and airlines, along with markets where customers may be more willing to pay for sustainable alternatives. Edybites spoons blend sorghum, corn and wheat flour to create a sturdy yet easy-to-bite alternative to plastic cutlery. There is another irony to solve, too. The spoon is edible, but it still needs to reach the customer intact. That means packaging it carefully against moisture and breakage. Sanghvi says the team is experimenting with paper-based packaging and ways to reduce plastic without compromising the product. For a startup trying to eliminate one disposable item, using plastic to protect that alternative is hardly an ideal solution. It is a problem the team is still working through. What happens when a spoon becomes part of the meal? Perhaps the most interesting thing about Edybites is that its sustainability pitch does not end with the word "biodegradable". It asks people to rethink what they consider waste in the first place. A conventional spoon has a very short life. It may spend a few minutes carrying a bite of food before being separated from the meal and sent to a bin. Edybites is trying to stretch that experience a little further: what if the spoon itself became the final bite? At scale, that could add up. Based on an estimated 2.5-3 grams of plastic in a conventional disposable spoon, Edybites estimates that every one lakh edible spoons could potentially displace around 250-300 kg of single-use plastic. At 10 lakh spoons, that works out to roughly 2.5-3 tonnes of potential plastic displacement. These are estimates of what could be displaced if the edible spoons replace plastic ones at that scale, rather than plastic waste already avoided by the startup. For Sanghvi, however, the number is only one part of the larger picture. He is particularly interested in what happens when children encounter such alternatives early. His hope is that edible or biodegradable options could eventually find their way into school canteens, hospitals, senior-care facilities and other places where disposable cutlery is used every day. And perhaps that is where Rai's Ganpati gathering offers a glimpse of what adoption can look like. Edybites has sold or distributed over 5,100 spoons and estimates that replacing one lakh plastic spoons could potentially prevent 250–300 kg of single-use plastic waste. The children simply needed to know they could eat the spoon. Once they did, the idea stopped being a sustainability lesson and became something much more familiar: a biscuit-like treat at the end of a meal. Rai has continued recommending the spoons at gatherings since that first experience, and her reason is simple. "We've got to be a flag bearer in our own way, no matter how small that change is," she says. For now, Edybites is still figuring out how to make that small change cheaper, easier to package, and practical at a much larger scale. But somewhere between a Mumbai kitchen, 88 failed attempts and a group of children happily chomping through their spoons after dessert, the idea has found its most convincing test yet. The spoon did not end up in the bin, it ended up being dessert. All images courtesy of Edybites team

items.descriptionOriginal: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most people moving through a train station aren’t really paying attention. They’re somewhere between where they left and where they’re going, phone out, eyes on the platform. Putting art there is an interesting bet; you’re trying to get someone to stop and look at something that might surprise and delight them, and that they had no intention of seeking out. NJ Transit has been doing this since 2019, when it launched the TRANSITional Art Project as a pilot at Newark Penn Station. Working with the New Jersey State Council on the Arts , it has since installed temporary exhibitions of murals and photography by New Jersey artists at seven more stations. The latest is now at Morris Plains Rail Station: a show called “ Tracks Through Time: Movement, History and Human Connection .” A show about the tracks themselves The subject matter has good timing. The exhibition looks at 250 years of American history through the lens of railroads , in the very stations where people still depend on those rails to get to work. It includes photography by Beyti Barbaros, murals by Jonathan Yumi, and a three-panel mural installation by Catherine Thurston. “Railroads helped to build this nation,” said NJ Transit President and CEO Kris Kolluri, “and as we mark 250 years of our shared history, there’s no better place to tell that story than in the very stations where the past and daily life intersect.” Art you don’t have to go looking for Nobody goes to a train station specifically to see art, but that might be at the heart of the reasoning for this whole project. Most people at a gallery already decided they wanted to be there. The commuter who glances up at a mural while waiting for the 8:14 didn’t, and that’s a different kind of encounter. Danielle Bursk, the New Jersey State Arts Council Director of Community Partnerships & Artist Services, put it this way: “Public art has the power to transform the places we move through every day into places where we can pause, connect , and see our communities in new ways.” The program also pays the artists. Some participants receive stipends toward the cost of developing a project in a transit space, which matters given how rarely public art comes with any budget at all. The program has now reached eight stations: Newark, Camden, Atlantic City, Trenton, New Brunswick, Summit, Rahway, and Morris Plains. Did this solution stand out? Όχι α…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Researchers at Columbia University Medical Center wanted to answer a specific question: what is the least amount of movement needed to offset the effects of prolonged sitting ? In 2023, they tested a range of options and found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy. Not a longer walk once an hour. Not standing more. The answer was as short and sweet as five minutes, every half hour. When NPR’s Body Electric ran that same challenge with more than 20,000 listeners, participants reported higher productivity and lower fatigue. Those results have real implications: adults in the United States average 9.5 hours of sitting per day, and the research linking prolonged sitting to fatigue, weight gain, back pain , and chronic disease is extensive. The five-minute walk is the most surprising and accessible finding, but there are four other adjustments, drawn from physical therapists, a biomechanist, and a professional ergonomist, that address what walking breaks alone can’t fix. For back pain: a three-dimensional spine rotation Slouching at a desk doesn’t just feel uncomfortable; it puts sustained stress on the middle section of the spine. Vinh Pham , a physical therapist, recommends a move he calls the 3D T-spine rotation. Stand and drop your right foot behind your left, about a foot apart. Hold your right arm straight up and your left arm behind you, as if shaking the hand of someone behind you. Then simultaneously drop both arms and twist toward your right foot, keeping them straight throughout. Return to the starting position, hold for two seconds, and repeat ten times before switching sides. The goal isn’t stretching in the conventional sense. It’s to get the spine comfortable with its full range of motion — side bending, backward bending, rotating — so those movements don’t cause pain when they come up in ordinary life. For eye strain: look somewhere else Digital eye strain happens when the eyes spend hours focused at close range. They turn inward to track a nearby screen, adjust their focus for short vision, and hold that position. Eye doctors say the result is often fatigue, headaches, or blurred vision. The simplest intervention is the one most people already know and skip: look away from the screen and focus on something distant. A full eye-muscle stretch goes further. That means moving your gaze deliberately through different positions to work muscles that stay locked during screen time . For restlessness: stop trying to find the right posture Katy Bowman , a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position , is direct on the idea that fidgeting is a signal, not a bad habit. It means your body needs to stop holding a static position, regardless of how ergonomically correct that position might be. Bowman and physical therapist Leada Malek , author of Science of Stretch , share a phrase common in their field: “Your best posture is your next posture.” Any position, held long enough, creates strain. The goal isn’t to find the correct one and maintain it; it’s to keep moving between positions. Sitting, standing, reclining, shifting. “Adaptive and dynamic,” as Malek describes it, and easy to move in and out of. For shoulder and neck aches: fix the monitor height first Professional ergonomist Meg Honan identifies one setup problem that causes more widespread discomfort than almost anything else: the “head down, arms up” configuration, where the screen is too low and the keyboard is too high. Bring your screen to eye level using books, a stand, or whatever is available. Lower your keyboard and mouse so you’re not shrugging to type. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, an external keyboard lets you lower your arms without losing screen height. Honan describes the head-down, arms-up position as a reliable setup for feeling “achy, sore and tired.” Getting the monitor to eye level is the single adjustment with the most downstream effect. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: Rosa Parks is known for her civil rights activism, not her cooking . But her handwritten pancake recipe is worth a look, not just as a historical document, but to see why it calls for a hearty helping of melted peanut butter. Written on the back of a bank deposit envelope, the recipe lives in the Library of Congress . On TikTok, Carlena Davis, a cook, author, and the creator of the Spilling the Sweet Tea TikTok account, tried out the recipe here and raved about it: Rosa Parks’ ‘Featherlite Pancakes’ recipe The handwritten recipe reads [edited for clarity]: Featherlite Pancakes Sift together: 1 cup flour 2 Tbsp baking powder 1/2 tsp salt 2 Tbsp sugar Mix: 1 egg 1 1/4 cup milk 1/3 cup peanut butter, melted 1 Tbsp shortening or oil Combine with dry ingredients. Cook at 275° on griddle. All in all, it’s a pretty standard pancake recipe, except for that unexpected melted peanut butter. What adding peanut butter does to a pancake recipe Many people put peanut butter on their pancakes; it’s less common to see peanut butter in the batter. What does adding peanut butter do? For one, adding peanut butter to pancakes makes them more filling. That can be great for growing kids or people who do a lot of physical work. Regular pancakes don’t have much protein or fat, so adding peanut butter beefs them up. Peanut butter also adds a rich flavor to the pancakes. Is it the secret to being “featherlite”? Perhaps. According to The Spruce , pancake texture depends on a mix of chemical reactions influenced by gas bubbles, heat, and viscosity. The fat in peanut butter could increase the pancake’s density, making it less fluffy. But it could also increase the batter’s viscosity, making it fluffier. So, it really depends on the mix of other ingredients. A woman carrying a stack of pancakes. Photo by Joy Real on Unsplash Modern peanut butter pancakes are much simpler The keto/paleo/gluten-free diet trends of the past decade have resulted in all kinds of altered recipes, some of which remove grains altogether. You can actually make a single serving of flour-free pancakes by combining: 1 small or 1/2 large banana 1 egg 1 Tbsp peanut butter 1/2 tsp baking powder Blend and cook in a pan like a regular pancake. These pancakes aren’t light and fluffy; they’re denser and crepey, but if you don’t mind a little banana-and-peanut-butter flavor, they’re quite good. (And there are lots of variations on this recipe. Some people add yogurt or cottage cheese; some use a little ground oats—they’re actually quite forgiving, so fun to experiment.) History’s recipes are often worth revisiting Today, we can find any recipe in seconds simply by Googling. Sure, you have to wade through someone’s entire life story to get to the recipe, but it’s still faster than finding the right cookbook and searching for the recipe you want. Online recipes also offer user ratings and reviews, so you can gauge how good a recipe is before you try it. However, there is something to be said for the joy of reading a recipe from someone who liked it enough to write it down by hand. There’s a story behind every envelope with a recipe written on it, like Rosa Parks’ pancakes. Did she have them at a friend’s house and ask to copy down the recipe? Did she invent it herself and finally write it out for others to copy? We may never know, but there’s something nostalgic and sweet about seeing Parks’ handwritten recipe, and even what looks like a drop of food on the envelope. You know a recipe is well-loved when it’s messy with ingredients. That’s something no online recipe can offer, no matter how long the story that accompanies it. items.descriptionOriginal: Hospice nurse Julie has shared tons of helpful , insightful , and even comforting videos on end-of-life care and death . Recently, she got candid about exactly what she would want to happen if she were diagnosed with dementia . She acknowledged that dementia comes in many forms and that no single approach works for everyone. But based on her years of watching patients and families navigate cognitive decline, she wanted to offer a general idea of how she would prepare. Her list included six things she would want done immediately following a diagnosis, while she still has plenty of cognitive ability to plan for such things herself. “A lot of people are gonna think this is harsh, but this is what I would want,” she said. No. 1: Establish DNR and DNI orders Hospital patient with a ‘DNR’ order. Photo credit: Canva DNR stands for “Do Not Resuscitate,” while DNI means “Do Not Intubate.” These medical orders tell healthcare providers not to do things like CPR, use a breathing tube, or use a ventilator, etc., should a patient’s heart stop beating or they stop breathing. For Julie, the decision comes down to the kind of care she would want as the dementia progresses. CPR and mechanical ventilation can be invasive, and she would prefer to allow a natural death rather than receive those interventions. No. 2: Say no to artificial nutrition Feeding tube. Photo credit: Canva Julie also said she would not want a feeding tube or to agree to assisted feeding if the dementia progressed to the point where she could not feed herself. In her view, that level of assistance would indicate that her quality of life had declined beyond what she would find acceptable. “I would rather cut my life short,” she said. According to GoodRx , studies indicate that tube feeding does not prolong life, improve quality of life, or prevent aspiration pneumonia in patients with severe dementia. They are more often designed as a temporary fix for shorter treatments, such as after a stroke, during cancer treatment, or while recovering from surgery. Julie did add the disclaimer that, in this situation, there would be a chance the disease has not advanced enough to truly mark the end of life. That means a person could be cutting their life short by starving to death and “feeling” that starvation. But in this scenario, the person would have had enough notice to be placed in hospice care and hopefully on some “comfort meds” so there wouldn’t have to be suffering. No. 3: Decline infection treatment Family surrounding man in hospital. Photo credit: Canva People with advanced dementia can develop complications such as aspiration pneumonia and urinary tract infections. If Julie found herself in this position, she would rather allow the infection to run its course than prolong her life with intense cognitive decline. Comfort-focused care options exist in these situations. For instance, administering Tylenol and morphine can manage symptoms like pain and achiness. This does not mean that infections should automatically go untreated for people with dementia. The right choice depends on the person’s preference, overall health, and care goals. No. 4: Start planning for the cost of care Older woman meeting with a financial advisor. Photo credit: Canva Julie also recommends thinking about the financial side of dementia as soon as possible. Hospice can cover many services for eligible people, including medical care, medications related to terminal illness, and support for patients and families through Medicare Part A , Medi-Cal, private insurance, or the VA. But hospice isn’t the same as round-the-clock custodial care. Generally, 24/7 care at home or room and board in a nursing facility is paid out of pocket. This makes long-term financial planning particularly important. Depending on the person’s needs and resources, care might eventually require family caregivers, paid home care, assisted living, or memory care in a skilled nursing facility. The National Institute on Aging also recommends making financial and long-term care plans early, while the person with dementia can still participate in those decisions. This ensures the individual’s voice guides critical legal and financial choices before cognitive decline limits their ability to make them. In addition to creating a budget, this includes setting up a durable power of attorney, creating a living will, and consulting an elder law attorney. No. 5: Plan the funeral Funeral. Photo credit: Canva While she can still choose for herself, Julie wants to decide whether she wants to be buried or cremated, whether she wants a funeral service, and what types of music or readings she might want included. It might feel strange to plan a funeral so far in advance, but doing so can take some of the burden off loved ones later, so they don’t have to guess. Especially if dementia eventually makes it difficult for the person to communicate these wishes. No. 6: Have a ‘living funeral’ Celebration of life. Photo credit: Canva Finally, Julie said she would want to “celebrate” her life while she could still fully participate. She knows that a dementia diagnosis would bring a natural “grieving process.” But rather than waiting until the disease had progressed, she would want to gather the people she loves and honor who she is at that moment. This could mean a big gathering or “living funeral,” as she phrased it. Or it could mean simply making more time for the people and activities that bring her joy. Whatever your wishes are, make them known For Julie, all these decisions come back to one thing: making them while she can still speak for herself. Of course, end-of-life care is a series of deeply personal decisions. A person with dementia may have very different wishes depending on their health, values, and disease stage. That’s why it’s important to discuss these choices with a doctor and loved ones while the person can still decide. That means learning about the specific diagnosis, talking with doctors and loved ones, and discussing what quality of life means to her before she may no longer be able to communicate those wishes. An advance directive can then put those preferences in writing. It lets a person document their wishes for future medical care if they become unable to make or communicate decisions. Depending on state law, it can also allow someone to designate a healthcare proxy or durable power of attorney to make medical decisions on their behalf. They can be filled out for free online. These conversations are never easy, with ourselves or with others. But having them early can give our loved ones and us clarity when it matters most. The post Hospice nurse shares the 6 things she’d do immediately after getting diagnosed with dementia appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: So you’re at a party and are introduced to someone you have never met before. How do you start the conversation? Many will ask, “What do you do for a living?” but that can make the other person uncomfortable if they feel their career isn’t terribly interesting. It also sounds a lot like you’re secretly asking: “How much money do you make?” You can also ask, “How was your day today?” but if the other person’s day was uneventful, this could be a real conversation dead-ender. The same goes for “What are you doing this weekend?” They may have no plans or feel uncomfortable sharing them. So, what question do you ask? Two guys chatting at a party. Photo credit: Canva What’s the best small talk question to ask? Terry Gross, the host of NPR’s popular Fresh Air podcast, has interviewed thousands of people, and she always asks: “So, tell me about yourself.” She says the genius of the four-word phrase is that “it allows you to start a conversation without the fear that you’re going to inadvertently make someone uncomfortable or self-conscious,” she said in a New York Times interview. “Posing a broad question lets people lead you to who they are.” The question lets the person being asked answer in a way that reflects what they really care about. It could be their profession, a hobby, or a cause they care about. Their answer will likely reflect their interests and reveal a lot about who they truly are. It also lets them avoid topics they don’t want to discuss and keeps you from making uncomfortable assumptions. If you’re preparing for interviews or think you’ll ever be asked, “Tell me about yourself,” you need to watch this. pic.twitter.com/5qf0xVMNLG — Akintola Steve (@Akintola_steve) July 26, 2026 Asking someone, “Tell me about yourself,” also plays into basic human biology. A Harvard study found that when people talk about themselves, it activates the brain region associated with rewards like food, money, and sex. We naturally enjoy talking about ourselves because it promotes social connection, and that’s what we’re trying to do with small talk, right? This question also works because studies show that when people meet someone new, they want to understand or relate to them beyond the initial context. So, say you’re at a party for a mutual friend’s birthday. The person you’ve met would also like to relate to you in another context, such as a shared interest or a professional connection. Sociologists call these “multiplex ties,” and sharing them with others is linked to greater well-being. Two women laughing together. Photo credit: Canva Be more likable with a few follow-up questions If you really want to seal the deal and make the person you’re speaking with like you, another Harvard study found that after you ask your introductory question (“Tell me about yourself”), if you ask two follow-up questions, people will rank you much more likable than if you asked the question and then turned the conversation around to yourself. Sometimes the simplest solution is the best one. You may feel a bit reluctant to ask such a simple question to kick off an interaction. But once the conversation gets flowing, you’ll have plenty of opportunities to ask thought-provoking questions and give interesting answers. It all starts with getting your conversation partner to start talking, and nothing gets people going quite like their favorite topic: themselves. items.descriptionOriginal: Residents at the Grace Village Retirement Community are no strangers to visits from emergency workers. Unfortunately, those visits are not always for the most uplifting reasons. This week, however, members of the Kosciusko County Sheriff’s Office stopped by the residence , simply to have coffee and tea and listen to residents’ rich tapestry of stories. Winona Lake, named for the nearby lake of the same name, is home to the retirement community. It sits in Kosciusko County, just outside Warsaw, Indiana, in a region sprinkled with lakes, ponds, and rivers . Photo Credit: Grace Village Activities Team Getting pampered When members of the Kosciusko County Sheriff’s Office visited the community, residents were thrilled they had come to share some hot drinks and have a lovely chat. Some deputies even gave mini-manicures, painting residents’ nails. WNDU (16 News Now) in South Bend reported that the deputies “sat down for a little coffee and pampering during their visit, painting residents’ nails and listening to their stories.” The Sheriff’s Office shared: “It’s a reminder that serving the community isn’t just about emergency or law enforcement. Sometimes it’s as simple as showing up and leaving behind a fresh coat of nail polish.” Upworthy spoke with David O’Connor , who works with nonprofits to share their stories. He spoke with Llesenia Simpson, activities director from the senior living facility. Simpson explained how it all went down: “We reached out in September to the Kosciusko County Sheriff’s Office and spoke with Doug Light about having a few officers join our residents for coffee and conversation planning for our October calendar.” Photo Credit: Grace Village Activities Team Pumpkin muffins and coffee Simpson described a typical morning. “Our residents typically spend that coffee hour reminiscing or listening to good music together, so when Doug agreed, we knew it would be a welcomed treat. Warsaw Starbucks in front of Meijer had actually donated pumpkin muffins and coffee for our visit.” Having their nails done was already on the schedule. “The day of, it was a full house in our Healthcare activity room. Several residents had asked to have their nails done before the officers arrived, and our team was working through that list when the officers walked in, tall, in uniform, and smiling ear to ear. Every resident’s face lit up. Even residents who are usually on the quieter side were bright-eyed and fully engaged,” Simpson continued. The Sheriff got the party started. “Sheriff Jim Smith was the first to put on gloves and ask one of our residents if he could polish her nails. She was delighted and, as I recall, replied, ‘Well, you sure can!’ None of it was planned. Once Sheriff Smith started, the nail care spread across the room, with officers and residents laughing and visiting the whole time,” Simpson recalled. ‘Pretty good at painting nails’ After being told he was a natural, Sheriff Smith answered, “I have girls and grandbabies at home, so I’ve gotten pretty good at painting nails.” Smith also said, “We want the public to know that the Sheriff’s Office is here not only to protect them, but also to work alongside them. Building trust, maintaining open communication, and creating positive interactions with our citizens are all important parts of effective law enforcement. At the end of the day, we are all part of the same community, and we are committed to making Kosciusko County a safe and welcoming place to live, work, and raise a family.” View this post on Instagram Building a community Sgt. Doug Light added: “As law enforcement officers, our responsibility goes beyond enforcing the law and responding to emergencies. It’s about building relationships, showing compassion, and reminding people that they are valued members of our community. “Visiting Grace Village gives us the opportunity to connect with our senior citizens, listen to their stories, share a smile, and maybe even paint a few fingernails. Sometimes, the most meaningful thing an officer can do is simply take the time to be present and let someone know they matter.” The post Police in a small Indiana town visited a senior community and painted the residents’ nails appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Actress Julia Stiles wowed the audience once again with a nostalgic nod to another of her beloved movie roles on last night’s Dancing With the Stars . Last week, Stiles performed a throwback routine to her 2001 movie Save the Last Dance , earning rave reviews. This week, she recreated an iconic dance from her 1999 movie 10 Things I Hate About You , in which she starred opposite the late Heath Ledger . Stiles and her partner, Ezra Sosa, performed a contemporary routine to Frankie Valli’s “Can’t Keep My Eyes Off You.” At the end of the performance, Stiles paid an emotional tribute to Ledger, leaving a rose as she stood before a photo of them from the film. She also surprised the DWTS audience by bringing the film’s original cast back together on the dance floor. Stiles performs “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You” In the video package before the performance, Stiles shared , “I learned a lot from Heath. He was so authentic. I have so many great memories, but I’m also sad because I really wish I could pick up the phone and be like, ‘Hey, dude. People really care about that movie. We did something special.'” After Stiles and Sosa were introduced, they began a beautifully choreographed dance to Valli’s hit famously featured in 10 Things I Hate About You . In the movie, Ledger’s character, high schooler Patrick Verona, plays the song over the loudspeaker at the school’s stadium to woo Stiles’ character, Kat Stratford. It’s a dance seared into Millennial memories, and Stiles and Sosa recreated it with sentimental flair. Stiles wore a sparkling blue dress (similar to the one she wore to prom in the film) and long, curly hair extensions that made her resemble her on-screen self. The routine copied many of Ledger’s bleacher dance moves in the film, culminating in a tearjerking tribute to the actor. View this post on Instagram Honoring Heath Ledger As the routine ended, Sosa left Stiles alone onstage, holding a red rose. She faced a large screen where a photo of Stiles and Ledger from 10 Things I Hate About You appeared. As the music faded, Stiles’ voice took over from one of the film’s most emotional and nostalgic scenes: when her character reads a poem in class about Ledger’s character. “I hate it when you’re not around, and the fact that you didn’t call. But mostly I hate the way that I don’t hate you. Not even close. Not even a little bit. Not even at all,” she says, as she places the rose at the foot of the steps for Ledger. Cast of 10 Things I Hate About You reunites After Stiles placed the rose, cast members from the film joined her on stage for an emotional ending to the performance. Actors Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Gabrielle Union, Larisa Oleynik, Andrew Keegan, and Susan May Pratt all stood with Stiles, holding hands. In a video shared on Instagram from before the show with the cast and Stiles, Union said, “We are here tonight to support our girl, Julia Stiles. She’s gonna kill it!” The performance earned roaring applause from the crowd, and the DWTS judges awarded Stiles and Sosa 36/40 points. Viewers respond The performance was a hit with 10 Things I Hate About You and Ledger fans, who shared their thoughts in the video’s comments section: “Crying the entire dance, lost it with the rose and the cast coming out. The loss of Heath hit so hard and this just brought back all the feels ” “They even incorporated Heath Ledger’s moves into the dance. I love that! And all the cast at the end… ” “OH MY GOSH! I’m SOBBING! Props to Ezra, bringing her movies to life again. He has done great work this season. Pure light and love by showcasing and recreating a small piece of filmography brilliance in a new dance. She deserved a 10s. My nostalgia cup runneth over tonight. Amazing dedication dance. Heath is looking down proud. Had to make us cry with the poem at the end. RIP Heath. ” “Joke’s on you, Julia. I had already planned on sobbing my damn eyes out today!!” “Julia you can’t have me sobbing like this. It’s not fair.” “didnt expect to see the cast there omggg im sobbing” “The end of the dance when the cast came together ” “Her prom dress ” The post Julia Stiles honors the late Heath Ledger with ’10 Things I Hate About You’ routine on ‘DWTS’ appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today Reading Time: 2 minutes 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today Making your home more sustainable doesn’t require expensive renovations or a complete lifestyle overhaul. In fact, some of the most effective changes are surprisingly simple, and you can start making them today. From the products you use to clean your kitchen to the materials you sleep under, everyday household choices can affect the environment. If you want to reduce waste, embrace more natural materials, and make your home a little greener, here are five sustainable swaps to consider. 1. Swap Disposable Cleaning Products for Reusable Alternatives Consider how many paper towels, disposable wipes, and plastic cleaning bottles you use in a typical month. These everyday essentials can create surprising waste, especially when you replace them constantly. Instead, consider switching to washable microfiber cloths, reusable cleaning pads, and refillable spray bottles . You can also explore concentrated cleaning solutions that require less packaging and are designed to be diluted at home. These small changes can reduce household waste while helping you save money over time. 2. Choose Natural Bedding Over Synthetic Materials Your bedroom is another great place to introduce more sustainable materials, especially in your bedding. Many conventional comforters contain synthetic polyester fillings derived from petroleum-based materials, which can contribute to plastic pollution. Replacing them with natural alternatives is a more environmentally conscious choice. An organic wool comforter offers a natural filling that provides warmth while allowing air to circulate and helping regulate temperature throughout the night. Wool is also renewable and biodegradable when untreated, making it an appealing option for anyone looking to reduce reliance on synthetic textiles. Your bedroom is a great place to introduce sustainable materials, especially in your bedding. Image: Home of Wool 3. Replace Single-Use Kitchen Products The kitchen is often one of the biggest sources of household waste, but it’s also one of the easiest places to make sustainable improvements. Instead of relying on plastic wrap, disposable sandwich bags, and single-use food containers, invest in reusable alternatives. Glass storage containers, washable silicone bags, and beeswax food wraps can help you cut down on unnecessary packaging. You could also swap disposable coffee pods for a reusable coffee filter or French press. Over time, these changes can noticeably reduce how much waste leaves your kitchen. 4. Switch to Energy-Efficient Lighting If you’re still using traditional incandescent light bulbs, switching to LED alternatives is a straightforward way to reduce household energy consumption. LED bulbs use significantly less electricity and generally last much longer than incandescent bulbs, so you need to replace them less often. This can help lower both your electricity bills and your home’s environmental footprint. You can also make better use of natural daylight by keeping windows unobstructed and arranging furniture to maximize available sunlight. 5. Choose Refillable Bathroom Essentials Bathrooms can quickly accumulate plastic packaging, particularly from shampoo, conditioner, hand soap, and body wash bottles. Switch to refillable products or solid alternatives, such as shampoo bars and bar soaps. Many brands now offer concentrated refills, so you can reuse existing containers instead of buying new plastic bottles every time. You might also replace disposable cotton rounds with washable alternatives and choose toothbrushes with replaceable heads to cut unnecessary waste. Start with one or two manageable swaps, build on them gradually, and you’ll soon discover that sustainable living can be both practical and rewarding. The post 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have developed a new way to quickly recycle electronic waste. Many electronic devices use flame-retardant plastic as casing in order to reduce the risk of electrical fires. This plastic is formulated using a metal called antimony along with organic bromide compounds. In fact, 39% of the world’s antimony is used to create flame-retardant plastics, most of which will eventually end up as part of the tens of millions of tons of electronic waste generated each year. Rice University’s James Tour recently published a study in Nature Chemical Engineering detailing an improved method to recover antimony from this electronic waste stream. “Antimony is a critical metal with a constrained supply,” says Tour, a professor of chemistry and corresponding author on the study. “My research team has adapted our flash Joule heating technique to quickly and effectively recover antimony from this plastic waste stream.” To recapture antimony from the plastic, it first has to be released from the plastic. This is, chemically, a challenging step. As the antimony is released, other toxic compounds, organic bromides, can form that are difficult to capture. “Conventionally heating the plastic releases the antimony in a volatile and difficult to collect form as well as creating and releasing hazardous organic bromide compounds,” says Leo Haoxin Ye, the first author of this paper and a graduate student at Rice. “Other options are risky or more impractical, such as using strong acids, organic solvents, or multistep treatment options.” The issue, the team thought, could be with the slowness of conventional heating, which allowed the elements to change forms or create new compounds. If they could adapt Tour’s flash Joule heating, which heats materials up to hundreds of degrees Celsius in a manner of milliseconds, they might be able to avoid some of the pitfalls of conventional heating while still releasing the antimony from the plastic. “We found flame-retardant plastic waste generated by our own laboratory, ground it up, and then placed it between two sheets of electrically heated carbon paper. We used ultrafast heating to pulse-heat it several times,” Ye says. “Then we held the plastic briefly at a high temperature, which allowed the antimony to evaporate and condense in a collection area.” The method, called isothermal-clamped flash Joule heating, was tested on three different types of flame-retardant plastic: a power-supply housing, a printed circuit board, and an electrical connector. From these, the team was able to recover approximately 90% of the antimony, while converting 83% of the bromide into hydrogen bromide, an inorganic compound that, while hazardous, is a valuable industrial chemical that can be captured with sodium hydroxide to form a stable salt. And the number of organic bromide compounds produced dramatically reduced, a result of the flash Joule heating’s speed. The plastic spent only 9.4 milliseconds in between 200-500 degrees Celsius, the temperature range in which organic bromide compounds form. “Isothermal-clamped flash Joule heating could improve the speed, safety, and practicality of antimony recovery from discarded flame-retardant plastics,” Tour says. “Given that the world is on track to produce 82 million metric tons of flame-retardant plastic waste by 2030, this represents an important step forward to conserving and reusing our critical antimony supply while also regenerating bromide salts for reuse.” This research was funded by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research and the US Army Corps of Engineers, ERDC. Source: Rice University The post New method can quickly recycle electronic waste appeared first on Futurity .

items.title: Τα ανθρώπινα νευρικά βλαστοκύτταρα είναι ευαίσθητα στις παραλλαγές του ιού COVID

Τα ευρήματα εγείρουν ανησυχίες σχετικά με τις πιθανές επιπτώσεις της μητρικής λοίμωξης COVID-19 στην πρώιμη ανάπτυξη του νευρικού συστήματος και υπογραμμίζουν τη σημασία της παρακολούθησης των παιδιών πρώην…
items.descriptionOriginal: Human neural stem cells that help form the brain and spinal cord are highly susceptible to SARS-CoV-2, including Omicron variants BA.1 and BA.2, according to new research. The findings raise concerns about the potential effects of maternal COVID-19 infection on early nervous system development and underscore the importance of monitoring children exposed to the virus before birth. The researchers, led by Prue Talbot, a professor of the graduate division in the Department of Molecular, Cell and Systems Biology, found that human neural stem cells were significantly more susceptible to infection by SARS-CoV-2 spike pseudoparticles—modified, non-replicating virus particles used to safely study infection—than undifferentiated human embryonic stem cells. The susceptibility was observed with the original viral spike as well as the two Omicron variants. “Our data clearly show that human neural stem cells are readily infected by SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus, including the currently prevalent Omicron variants,” Talbot says. Neural stem cells emerge from the ectoderm, an early embryonic tissue that gives rise to the central nervous system. Because these cells help establish the foundation for the brain and spinal cord, infection during early development could have consequences ranging from pregnancy loss and severe developmental abnormalities to more subtle changes that may not be apparent at birth. “Such subtle damage might only appear years later as learning, behavioral, or cognitive difficulties,” says Ann Song, a postdoctoral researcher in Talbot’s lab and the first author of the study in PLOS One . The transmission of SARS-CoV-2 from mother to fetus has been documented, including during the first trimester. Children exposed to the virus in utero are now reaching ages at which potential neurodevelopmental differences can be assessed. The researchers also noted that their findings are consistent with a large health-record study linking maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection to an increased risk of a neurodevelopmental diagnosis in children by age 3. To investigate how the virus might enter developing neural cells, the team differentiated human embryonic stem cells into neural stem cells and exposed them to the pseudoparticles. The experiments showed that Omicron pseudoparticles entered neural stem cells primarily through endocytosis, a process in which cells engulf external material. The researchers found that blocking this pathway with the compound filipin reduced viral entry by approximately 75% to 85%. The team also found that neural stem cells have a relatively sparse layer of sugar molecules on their surfaces. Removing these sugar groups increased pseudoparticle entry twofold to fourfold, suggesting that the cell-surface sugar layer may help limit viral access. The research addresses a question that cannot readily be investigated through experiments in pregnant women: whether early precursors of the nervous system are vulnerable to SARS-CoV-2. Although fetal transmission has been documented, the susceptibility of these early developmental cells has been less clear. “Our data emphasize the need for monitoring children exposed in utero to SARS-CoV-2 for evidence of deficiencies in the central nervous system,” Song says. Talbot says the findings do not establish that infection of neural stem cells by the pseudovirus causes neurological harm in human pregnancies. “Further research will be needed to determine whether and how infection at these early stages affects brain development,” she says. The study was funded by a UCR Academic Senate Committee on Research grant, an Academic Merit Fellowship, a Yvonne Danielson Endowed Graduate Award, a UCR Graduate Division Dissertation Completion Fellowship Award, and the Tobacco-Related Disease Research Program. Source: UC Riverside The post Human neural stem cells are susceptible to COVID virus variants appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: He’s the first Indian to win the Oskar Klein Medal, yet he still cycles to work. His story is as much about simplicity as it is about extraordinary scientific achievement. Meet Kolkata-born theoretical physicist Ashoke Sen, whose pioneering research in string theory and black hole physics has helped shape our understanding of the universe. After studying at Presidency College and IIT Kanpur and pursuing doctoral research in the United States, he returned to India to continue his scientific journey. In 2012, Sen received the $3 million Fundamental Physics Prize for his contributions to string theory. In 2026, he made history by becoming the first Indian physicist to receive the Oskar Klein Medal, recognising his influential work in theoretical physics. Despite global recognition and some of the field’s highest honours, Sen’s story reminds us that scientific greatness is measured by curiosity, dedication and the ideas we contribute, not by outward displays of success. His journey continues to inspire young Indians to pursue knowledge and push the boundaries of human understanding. Know a student who’s drawn to physics?
